title: Words, song and images (CCC 1153–1162)
hook: the one who sings prays twice, as the saying goes

segments.voice: Yesterday, signs and symbols: water, oil, bread, wine and light. Your line was creation speaks. What ordinary thing said something to you before you used it? Day one thousand ninety.

The one who sings prays twice. That's an old saying as the Catechism gives it, and it credits the line to Saint Augustine. There's something to it. A sentence spoken once is easy to lose by lunch. A sentence sung tends to stay, sometimes for years, attached to a tune that can come back at a red light or in the shower. Yesterday the Catechism talked about things, water, oil and bread. Today it turns to the other material the liturgy is made of: words spoken, words sung, and pictures on the walls.
screen: `THE ONE WHO SINGS PRAYS TWICE.` → `A SUNG LINE STAYS.` → `WORDS, SONG, PICTURES.`

segments.voice: First, words. The Catechism describes the liturgy as a meeting, a conversation between God and his people, carried by actions and words together. That's why every sacrament comes with words. The water of baptism is poured while words are said. The Word of God is read aloud, and the Catechism says the books, the place of reading, the way it's read and the listening all matter. Second, song. Saint Paul tells the Ephesians to speak to one another "in psalms, and hymns, and spiritual canticles, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord." The Catechism sets that verse beside the saying about praying twice, and beside a story from Augustine's own life. In the days of his baptism in Milan, Augustine heard the church's hymns, and he wept. The voices flowed into his ears, he wrote, and the truth into his heart. The Catechism says the Church's music should be beautiful, should help people pray, and should let the whole gathering join in, not just the choir. Third, images. Here the Catechism makes a careful argument. The invisible God can't be pictured. But in Jesus, Catholics believe, God became flesh and could be seen. So an image of Christ isn't a guess at the invisible. It points to someone who was really seen. The Church honors images of Christ, Mary, the angels and the saints, and elsewhere the Catechism says the honor passes through the picture to the one pictured. Fourth, they work together. Word, song and image all say the same thing in different ways, to the ear, the voice, the eye. Some people are moved by an argument. Augustine, by his own account, was moved to tears by a hymn.
screen: `A CONVERSATION OF WORDS AND ACTIONS.` · `PSALMS, AND HYMNS, AND SPIRITUAL CANTICLES.` · `AUGUSTINE WEPT AT THE HYMNS.` · `GOD BECAME FLESH, AND COULD BE SEEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing a line of a hymn. Settle, and breathe. Let one song come back to you, a hymn, a carol, a psalm, something sung at a wedding or a funeral or in a school assembly long ago. Find just one line of it. Then sing it, softly, out loud if you can, or under your breath if you can't. Don't worry about the key. Sing it a second time, slower, and notice what the words say. If you pray, you can let the line be your prayer. If you don't, let it be a way of remembering the people you once sang it with. The bell holds the time.
Words. In the liturgy, words spoken and sung carry the meeting between God and his people, together with actions and images that point to Christ. Today's word.
Your line: sing it. Today, sing one line of something, anything, in the car or the kitchen, and let it count twice. Day one thousand ninety.

howItsDone: At Mass Catholics hear scripture read aloud, sing psalms and hymns, and pray in churches decorated with images of Christ, Mary and the saints; Eastern Catholics venerate icons.

fork.setup: you're Augustine, in the days of your baptism, standing in the church in Milan as the hymns begin. what happens?
options: you argue with the bishop about the words
you weep, as the truth flows into your heart
fork.reveal: he wept. the voices flowed into his ears, he wrote, and the truth into his heart.

trapdoor: what you thought: the songs and pictures are decoration around the real prayer.
what it means: in the liturgy, words, song and images all carry the meeting between God and his people.
what a scholar hears: the Catechism defends images from the Incarnation: the invisible God became flesh and could be seen.

notes: CCC paraphrased (1153 the celebration as a meeting and dialogue through actions and words; 1154 the Liturgy of the Word, the lectionary, ambo, proclamation and listening; 1155 word and action inseparable; 1156 Ephesians 5:19 and 'he who sings prays twice' credited to Augustine; 1157 beauty, unanimous participation, and Augustine weeping at the hymns in Milan; 1159 images and the Incarnation; 1161 images of Christ, Mary, angels and saints). Confirm.

'The one who sings prays twice': the CCC credits it to Augustine; some scholars question whether Augustine wrote it in this form. The hook keeps it as 'an old saying' that 'the Catechism credits' to him. Confirm.
'The honor passes through the picture to the one pictured' is the principle of CCC 2132 (and the Second Council of Nicaea), slightly outside this section's range; confirm or cut.
Augustine's Confessions IX.6.14 paraphrased (Pusey 1838 is public domain but exact wording not checked). Confirm.
howItsDone mentions Eastern Catholics and icons; confirm.

Editor pass: factual fix: Augustine's weeping at the hymns (Confessions IX.6.14) comes in his account of the days after his baptism, not before it; teach and fork setup corrected, and the closing 'come to faith through an argument' contrast reworded to match. Hook no longer opens 'Here's...' (day 1085's opener) and the Augustine credit is no longer repeated in the teach. The honor-passes-to-the-one-pictured principle is now marked 'elsewhere' and CCC 2132 added to sources.
